chapter.name: Triangles
chapter.blurb: Two figures with the same shape but not necessarily the same size are similar -- circles, squares and equilateral triangles always are, but a general quadrilateral needs both equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides to qualify. The chapter builds this idea into triangles specifically, opening with Thales' Basic Proportionality Theorem (a line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides in the same ratio) and its converse, then develops three criteria -- AAA/AA, SSS and SAS -- for declaring two triangles similar without checking all six corresponding parts, applying them to medians, altitudes, angle bisectors and indirect-measurement problems such as a girl's lamp-post shadow. This rationalized edition closes with the summary and a brief unproved note on the RHS similarity criterion; it does not cover areas of similar triangles or the Pythagoras theorem, which are not part of this chapter here.

concepts.name: Similar figures: meaning and conditions for similarity of polygons
concepts.description: Two figures having the same shape but not necessarily the same size are similar; congruent figures are always similar but similar figures need not be congruent; two polygons with the same number of sides are similar only when both their corresponding angles are equal AND their corresponding sides are proportional (the scale factor) -- neither condition alone is sufficient.
concepts.idea: Similar figures look exactly alike in shape, just enlarged or shrunk by a fixed scale factor.
concepts.rule: Two polygons of the same number of sides are similar if and only if (i) their corresponding angles are equal, and (ii) their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (the scale factor, also called the representative fraction). All circles are similar to each other, all squares are similar to each other, and all equilateral triangles are similar to each other, regardless of size.
concepts.example: A square of side 2 cm and a rectangle of sides 2 cm by 4 cm have all angles equal (90 degrees each) but sides not in the same ratio, so they are not similar (Fig 6.6, pp.77-78). A square of side 3 cm and a rhombus of side 3 cm with a 60 degree angle have all sides in the same ratio (1:1) but angles not equal, so they are not similar either (Fig 6.7, p.78).

concepts.name: Basic Proportionality Theorem (Thales Theorem): statement, proof and direct application
concepts.description: Theorem 6.1 (Basic Proportionality Theorem / Thales Theorem): a line parallel to one side of a triangle, intersecting the other two sides at distinct points, divides those two sides in the same ratio; its proof using areas of triangles on the same base and between the same parallels; direct use to find an unknown length.
concepts.idea: A line parallel to one side of a triangle cuts off a smaller copy of the triangle at the top, so it must split the other two sides in exactly the same ratio.
concepts.rule: If DE is parallel to BC in triangle ABC, with D on AB and E on AC, then AD/DB = AE/EC (Theorem 6.1). Proof idea: join BE and CD; draw DM perpendicular to AC and EN perpendicular to AB; ar(ADE)/ar(BDE) = AD/DB and ar(ADE)/ar(DEC) = AE/EC (triangles sharing a height); since ar(BDE) = ar(DEC) (same base DE, between the same parallels BC and DE), AD/DB = AE/EC.
concepts.example: In triangle ABC, DE is parallel to BC, D on AB, E on AC, with AD = 1.8 cm, DB = 5.4 cm, AE = 1.2 cm; then EC = AE x DB/AD = 3.6 cm. Example 1 (p.81): if DE is parallel to BC, cutting AB at D and AC at E, then AD/AB = AE/AC.

concepts.name: Converse of the Basic Proportionality Theorem and its applications
concepts.description: Theorem 6.2 (converse of BPT): if a line divides two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, it is parallel to the third side; proof idea via a coincidence argument; corollaries -- the midpoint theorem and its converse; using the converse (and AAA) for trapezium diagonal ratios; Examples 2 and 3.
concepts.idea: If a line splits two sides of a triangle in exactly the same ratio, it has no choice but to run parallel to the third side.
concepts.rule: If AD/DB = AE/EC for points D on AB and E on AC, then DE is parallel to BC (Theorem 6.2). Proof idea: assume a different line DE' is parallel to BC; then AD/DB = AE'/E'C by Theorem 6.1; combined with the given AD/DB = AE/EC, this forces AE/EC = AE'/E'C, and adding 1 to both sides shows E and E' must coincide, so DE itself is parallel to BC.
concepts.example: Midpoint theorem: if D and E are midpoints of AB and AC, then AD/DB = AE/EC = 1, so DE is parallel to BC. Example 3 (p.83): in triangle PQR, PS/SQ = PT/TR and angle PST = angle PRQ; since PS/SQ = PT/TR, ST is parallel to QR by the converse, so angle PST = angle PQR (corresponding angles); combined with angle PST = angle PRQ, this gives angle PRQ = angle PQR, so PQ = PR (isosceles).

concepts.name: Applying similarity criteria: medians, altitudes, bisectors and indirect measurement
concepts.description: Combining the similarity criteria across multi-step proofs -- Example 8 (medians CM and RN of similar triangles ABC and PQR: proving AMC~PNR by SAS, then CM/RN=AB/PQ, then CMB~RNQ by SSS); the trapezium-diagonal result reached via AAA directly, as a second route to the fact proved differently in concept 6.3; indirect measurement (heights and distances via shadows, extending Example 7).
concepts.idea: Once two triangles are known to be similar, their medians, altitudes and angle bisectors inherit the same scale factor, which is what makes real-world height-and-distance measurement by shadows possible.
concepts.rule: If triangle ABC ~ triangle PQR, then the ratio of any pair of corresponding medians, altitudes or angle bisectors equals the ratio of corresponding sides. Proving such results typically chains two similarity criteria together: first SAS or AA (using half a known side and the given angle) to relate two smaller triangles, then SSS or the ratio itself to relate the two triangles formed by the cevian.
concepts.example: Example 8 (pp.93-94): CM and RN are medians of similar triangles ABC and PQR; since AB = 2AM and PQ = 2PN, triangle AMC ~ triangle PNR by SAS, giving CM/RN = CA/RP = AB/PQ; then triangle CMB ~ triangle RNQ by SSS, using CM/RN = BC/QR = BM/QN. Exercise 6.3 Q3: diagonals AC, BD of trapezium ABCD (AB parallel to DC) meet at O; triangle AOB ~ triangle COD by AAA (alternate angles OAB=OCD, OBA=ODC, plus the vertical angle at O), giving OA/OC = OB/OD.

questions.q: A classmate says: 'Once you know triangle ABC ~ triangle PQR, every single line segment you can draw inside triangle ABC will automatically be in the same ratio to some corresponding segment in triangle PQR, not just medians, altitudes or bisectors.' Evaluate this claim.
questions.a: The claim is too broad to accept without qualification. It is true for segments that have a clearly defined corresponding version in the other triangle by the similarity's own correspondence (such as medians to corresponding vertices, altitudes to corresponding sides, or angle bisectors of corresponding angles) -- these are indeed always in the same ratio as the sides, as Example 8 shows for medians. However, an arbitrary line segment drawn inside triangle ABC with no defined correspondence in triangle PQR has no meaningful corresponding segment to compare it with, so the claim cannot be applied blindly to any arbitrary segment.
s: States the claim needs qualification rather than being simply true
Explains it holds for segments with a clear correspondence (e.g. medians, altitudes, bisectors, as in Example 8), but not for an arbitrary segment with no defined counterpart in the other triangle
